newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen separatist leader urges reconciliation.
newsitem.headline: Chechen separatist leader urges reconciliation.

text.p: Chechen separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev, struggling to cement a shaky peace in his breakaway region, has urged his people to show tolerance and to forgive their enemies, Itar-Tass news agency said on Tuesday.

However Yandarbiyev's postponement of a planned visit to Moscow and the death of six Russian soldiers in a landmine explosion on Tuesday cast a shadow over his efforts to keep the peace process on track and provoked an angry Russian reaction.
"It is practically impossible to build up an independent state in Chechnya without mutual forgiveness and concord," Tass quoted Yandarbiyev as telling Chechen television on Monday.
He said Chechens should draw confidence from the peace deal, clinched with the Kremlin's security supremo Alexander Lebed on August 31, return to their homes and start preparing for winter.
Under the deal all Chechens who collaborated with the pro-Moscow administration in the capital Grozny have been amnestied and should not be persecuted, Yandarbiyev said.
However he warned his political opponents in the mountainous southern region that he would deal ruthlessly with any attempts to undermine the peace accord.

His words came shortly before a landmine killed six Russian interior ministry soldiers travelling in an armoured personnel carrier in Dagestan, an ethnically mixed Russian region neighbouring Chechnya, Tass reported.

Russia reacted swiftly to the incident. "This is a crude provocation, aimed at the destabilisation of the atmosphere in the region," the commander of Russian forces in Chechnya, General Vyacheslav Tikhomirov, told Interfax news agency.
Tass described the situation in Chechnya as tough and said one Russian soldier had been killed there on Monday by a sniper.

Tens of thousands of people have been killed in Chechnya since President Boris Yeltsin, who is now in hospital preparing for heart surgery, sent troops there in December 1994 to quell an independence bid.
Yandarbiyev, a 44-year-old writer, took over the separatists' self-styled presidency in April after Dzhokhar Dudayev was reported killed in a rocket attack.

He said he had postponed a trip to Moscow this week because of the need to prepare more thoroughly for planned talks with Lebed and a possible meeting with Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin. No new date has been set for the visit.
The peace deal provides for the withdrawal of Russian troops and postponement of a decision on the region's status. The truce accompanying the accord has generally held since its signing.
Yeltsin's press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky praised a decision by the Council of Europe on Monday to shelve a planned discussion of the Chechen issue.

The decision by the Council, which promotes human rights and democracy across Europe, came after Lebed and Chechen separatist chief of staff Aslan Maskhadov spurned an invitation to discuss their peace agreement with the 39-nation group.

"The refusal to discuss the Chechen issue is on the one hand a success for Russian diplomacy and our parliamentarians and on the other a sensible decision of the European parliamentarians," Yastrzhembsky told the Ekho Moskvy radio station.
A lower-ranking Chechen delegation went instead to the Council headquarters in the French city of Strasbourg for informal talks with individual parliamentarians.
Moscow, which joined the Council of Europe in February after pledging to seek a peaceful settlement in Chechnya, had blasted the invitation to Maskhadov as interference in Russian affairs.
